# Section A — Read the verdict

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement about the positive integers $a$, $b$ and $n$:

> $(*)$: $ab$ is divisible by $n$

The condition "either $a$ or $b$ is divisible by $n$" is:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** necessary but not sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** sufficient but not necessary for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** necessary and sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** not necessary and not sufficient for $(*)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** Call the condition $C$. Test the two arrows one at a time.

**Is $C$ sufficient?** That asks whether $C\Rightarrow(*)$. Suppose $a$ is divisible by $n$, so $a=nk$ for some
integer $k$. Then

$$ab=nk\cdot b=n(kb),$$

which is a multiple of $n$. The same works if $b$ is the multiple. So $C$ is **sufficient**.

**Is $C$ necessary?** That asks whether $(*)\Rightarrow C$. Try a value of $n$ that is not prime. With $n=4$ and
$a=b=2$:

$$ab=4\text{ is divisible by }4,\qquad\text{but neither }a\text{ nor }b\text{ is.}$$

So $(*)$ holds while $C$ fails, and $C$ is **not necessary**.

**Why the other options fail.** A and C both claim necessity, which $a=b=2$, $n=4$ destroys. D denies sufficiency,
which the short proof above establishes.

*The tempting wrong answer is C: the reverse arrow does hold when $n$ is prime, but the question never says $n$ is
prime.*
:::

---

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
A list consists of $n$ integers.

Consider the following statements:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**P:** $n$ is odd.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Q:** The median of the list is one of the numbers in the list.

Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** P is necessary and sufficient for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** P is necessary but not sufficient for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** P is sufficient but not necessary for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** P is not necessary and not sufficient for Q.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

**Is P sufficient for Q?** That asks whether P $\Rightarrow$ Q. If $n$ is odd, then after sorting there is a single
middle entry. The median **is** that entry, so it is certainly in the list. **Yes.**

**Is P necessary for Q?** That asks whether Q $\Rightarrow$ P. We need a list with Q true and P false, so an
even-length list whose median is in the list. When $n$ is even the median is the mean of the two middle entries,
so make those two equal:

$$1,\ 2,\ 2,\ 3\quad\text{has median }\frac{2+2}{2}=2,\text{ which is in the list.}$$

Here Q is true and $n=4$ is even, so **no**.

**Why the other options fail.** A and B claim necessity, which the list above breaks. D denies sufficiency, which
the single middle entry establishes.
:::

---

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
A student is chosen at random from a class. Each student is equally likely to be chosen.

Which of the following conditions is/are **necessary** for the probability that the student wears glasses to equal
$\dfrac{4}{15}$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; Exactly $11$ students in the class do not wear glasses.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The number of students in the class is divisible by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The class contains $30$ students, and $8$ of them wear glasses.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** A necessary condition must hold in **every** class that has the probability $\tfrac{4}{15}$. So first list
those classes.

**Step 1: which classes have probability $\tfrac4{15}$?** With $N$ students, the number wearing glasses is
$\tfrac{4}{15}N$, and this must be a whole number. Since $\tfrac4{15}$ is in lowest terms, $N$ must be a multiple of
$15$:

| $N$ | wear glasses | do not |
|---|---|---|
| $15$ | $4$ | $11$ |
| $30$ | $8$ | $22$ |
| $45$ | $12$ | $33$ |

**Step 2: test each condition against every row.**

- **I** fails in the row $N=30$, which has $22$ students without glasses. Not necessary.
- **II** holds in every row, because a multiple of $15$ is a multiple of $3$. **Necessary.**
- **III** fails in the row $N=15$. Not necessary.

So only II is necessary.

*Notice that II is nowhere near sufficient, since a class of $3$ cannot have probability $\tfrac4{15}$. That does not
matter: the question asks only for necessary. III is the trap, because it is* sufficient *rather than necessary.*
:::

---

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set A · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
A child is chosen at random from a group. Each child is equally likely to be chosen.

Which of the following conditions is/are **necessary** for the probability that the child has a pet to equal exactly
$\dfrac{4}{9}$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; Exactly $5$ children in the group do not have a pet.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The number of children in the group is divisible by $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The number of children in the group with a pet is divisible by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** Same method as the previous question: list the groups with probability $\tfrac49$, then test each condition
against all of them.

**Step 1: the groups.** With $N$ children, $\tfrac49N$ must be a whole number, so $N$ is a multiple of $9$:

| $N$ | have a pet | do not |
|---|---|---|
| $9$ | $4$ | $5$ |
| $18$ | $8$ | $10$ |

**Step 2: test each condition.** The group of $N=9$ alone breaks II and III, and $N=18$ breaks I.

- **I** fails at $N=18$, where $10$ children have no pet.
- **II** fails at $N=9$, because $4$ does not divide $9$.
- **III** fails at $N=9$, because $3$ does not divide $4$.

None of them is necessary.

*The $4$ in II and the $3$ in III are planted: the numbers look connected to $\tfrac49$ without following from it.
The one consequence that does follow is "$N$ is divisible by $9$", and it is not on the list.*
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
Let $x$ be a real number.

Which one of the following statements is a **sufficient** condition for exactly three of the other four statements?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $x\ge0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $x=1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $x=0$ or $x=1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $x\ge0$ or $x\le1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $x\ge0$ and $x\le1$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** "$X$ is sufficient for $Y$" means every $x$ in $X$ is also in $Y$. So turn each statement into a set.

| | Statement | Set |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $x\ge0$ | $[0,\infty)$ |
| **B** | $x=1$ | $\{1\}$ |
| **C** | $x=0$ or $x=1$ | $\{0,1\}$ |
| **D** | $x\ge0$ **or** $x\le1$ | every real number |
| **E** | $x\ge0$ **and** $x\le1$ | $[0,1]$ |

**D** needs care: every real number satisfies at least one of $x\ge0$ and $x\le1$, so D is always true and is implied
by everything.

**Now count, for each statement, how many of the others contain it.**

| | Contained in | Count |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | D only | $1$ |
| **B** | A, C, D, E | $4$ |
| **C** | A, D, E (not B, since $x=0$ fails) | $3$ |
| **D** | none of them (take $x=-5$) | $0$ |
| **E** | A, D | $2$ |

Only C reaches exactly three.

*B is the near miss: it is sufficient for all four, which is not "exactly three".*
:::

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
Let $x$ and $y$ be non-zero real numbers with $x\neq y$.

Which one of the following statements is both **necessary and sufficient** for $x<y$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $y^{-1/3}<x^{-1/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $y^{1/5}<x^{1/5}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $x^{2/3}<y^{2/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $y^{2/3}<x^{2/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $|x|^{1/3}<|y|^{1/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $x^{-1/3}<y^{-1/3}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $x^{1/5}<y^{1/5}$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G.** "Necessary and sufficient" means the option must be **equivalent** to $x<y$.

**Why G works.** The fifth root is defined for every real number, and $t\mapsto t^{1/5}$ is strictly increasing on all
of $\mathbb R$. A strictly increasing function preserves order in both directions, so

$$x<y\iff x^{1/5}<y^{1/5}.$$

**Why the others fail.** Each option must at least follow from $x<y$. So for each one, find a pair with $x<y$ where
the option is false.

| Option | Pair with $x<y$ | What goes wrong |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $x=-1,\ y=1$ | $y^{-1/3}=1$ and $x^{-1/3}=-1$, and $1<-1$ is false |
| **B** | $x=1,\ y=2$ | it claims $2^{1/5}<1$ |
| **C** | $x=-8,\ y=-1$ | $x^{2/3}=4$ and $y^{2/3}=1$, and $4<1$ is false |
| **D** | $x=1,\ y=8$ | $y^{2/3}=4$ and $x^{2/3}=1$, and $4<1$ is false |
| **E** | $x=-8,\ y=-1$ | $|x|^{1/3}=2$ and $|y|^{1/3}=1$, and $2<1$ is false |
| **F** | $x=1,\ y=8$ | $x^{-1/3}=1$ and $y^{-1/3}=\tfrac12$, and $1<\tfrac12$ is false |

*Even powers (C, D) and absolute values (E) forget the sign, while reciprocals (A, F) reverse order on each side of
$0$ and jump across it. Only an odd root is increasing everywhere.*
:::

---

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
A TMUA question asks candidates to identify which one of the conditions below is a **sufficient but not necessary**
condition for some statement $P$, concerning a real number $x$, to hold.

Friedrich Gauss, sitting the exam, noticed to his delight that the examiner has designed the question poorly, and the
correct option can be deduced without knowing or examining $P$ in the slightest!

Which is the correct option?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $|x-2|<2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $x^{2}-5x+6<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\log(x-2)$ is defined

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $|x-2|<1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $x$ can be any real number
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** The key fact: **a condition inside a correct option is also correct.**

**Step 1: the general argument.** Suppose $Q$ is sufficient but not necessary for $P$, and $R$ is a condition with
$R\Rightarrow Q$.

- $R$ is sufficient for $P$, because $R\Rightarrow Q\Rightarrow P$.
- $R$ is not necessary for $P$. Since $Q$ is not necessary, some $x$ has $P$ true and $Q$ false. As $R\Rightarrow Q$,
  that same $x$ has $R$ false too.

So if $Q$ is a correct option and $R$ implies $Q$, then $R$ is correct as well.

**Step 2: write each option as a set.**

| | Option | Set |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\lvert x-2\rvert<2$ | $(0,4)$ |
| **B** | $(x-2)(x-3)<0$ | $(2,3)$ |
| **C** | $x-2>0$ | $(2,\infty)$ |
| **D** | $\lvert x-2\rvert<1$ | $(1,3)$ |
| **E** | any real $x$ | $\mathbb R$ |

**Step 3: finish.** The set $(2,3)$ lies inside each of the other four, so B implies all of them. If any other option
were correct, B would be correct too, giving two correct answers. There is only one, so it must be B.

*This is a real exam habit: on a "sufficient but not necessary" question, the strongest option is the only one that can
be unique.*
:::

# Section B — Find the exact condition

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
The graph of the line $ax+by=c$ is drawn, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are real non-zero constants.

Which one of the following is a **necessary** but **not sufficient** condition for the line to have a positive gradient
**and** a positive $y$-intercept?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\dfrac cb>0$ and $\dfrac ab<0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\dfrac cb<0$ and $\dfrac ab>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $a>b>c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $a<b<c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $a$ and $c$ have opposite signs

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $a$ and $c$ have the same sign
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.** Find the exact condition first.

**Step 1: rearrange.** From $by=-ax+c$,

$$y=-\frac abx+\frac cb,$$

so the gradient is $-\dfrac ab$ and the $y$-intercept is $\dfrac cb$.

**Step 2: the exact condition.** Both are positive exactly when

$$\frac ab<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac cb>0 .$$

That is option **A**, word for word, so A is necessary **and** sufficient. It is not what was asked.

**Step 3: necessity of E.** From Step 2, $a$ has the opposite sign to $b$, and $c$ has the same sign as $b$. So $a$ and
$c$ have opposite signs. E is **necessary**.

**Step 4: E is not sufficient.** Opposite signs for $a$ and $c$ say nothing about $b$. Take $a=1$, $b=1$, $c=-1$. The line
is $y=-x-1$, with gradient $-1$ and intercept $-1$, both negative.

**The other options.**

- **B** says the intercept is negative, so it contradicts the requirement. Not necessary.
- **C** is not necessary: $a=1$, $b=-2$, $c=-1$ gives $y=\tfrac12x+\tfrac12$, which qualifies, but $a>b>c$ fails since
  $-2<-1$.
- **D** is not necessary: $a=-1$, $b=2$, $c=1$ gives $y=\tfrac12x+\tfrac12$, which qualifies, but $a<b<c$ fails since
  $2>1$.
- **F** contradicts Step 3. Not necessary.
:::

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
A circle has equation

$$x^{2}+ax+y^{2}+by+c=0$$

where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are non-zero real constants.

Which one of the following is a **necessary and sufficient** condition for the circle to be tangent to the $y$-axis?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $a^{2}=4c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $b^{2}=4c$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\dfrac a2=\sqrt{\dfrac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\dfrac b2=\sqrt{\dfrac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $-\dfrac a2=\sqrt{\dfrac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $-\dfrac b2=\sqrt{\dfrac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c}$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.**

**Step 1: complete the square.**

$$\left(x+\tfrac a2\right)^{2}+\left(y+\tfrac b2\right)^{2}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c,$$

so the centre is $\left(-\tfrac a2,-\tfrac b2\right)$ and $r^{2}=\dfrac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c$.

**Step 2: what tangency means.** The circle touches the $y$-axis exactly when the radius equals the distance from the
centre to the axis, and that distance is $\left|\tfrac a2\right|$. It is not simply $-\tfrac a2$ or $\tfrac a2$, because the
centre can be on either side:

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,300)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4,3.8))
for cx,col,lab in [(-1,'#1f77b4','$a=2$: centre on the left'),(1,'#d62728','$a=-2$: centre on the right')]:
    ax.plot(cx+np.cos(t),-2+np.sin(t),color=col,lw=2,label=lab)
    ax.plot([cx],[-2],'o',color=col,ms=4)
ax.axvline(0,color='0.25',lw=1.2); ax.axhline(0,color='0.25',lw=1.2)
ax.set_xlim(-3,3); ax.set_ylim(-3.4,2.0); ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='upper center',ncol=1)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Step 3: square.** Both sides are non-negative, so squaring loses nothing:

$$\frac{a^{2}}{4}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{4}-c .$$

The $\tfrac{a^{2}}{4}$ cancels, leaving $0=\tfrac{b^{2}}{4}-c$, so $\boxed{b^{2}=4c}$.

*Quick check.* Put $x=0$ in the circle: $y^{2}+by+c=0$. Tangency means a repeated root, so the discriminant
$b^{2}-4c$ must be $0$. Same condition.

**The other options.**

- **A**, $a^{2}=4c$, is the condition for tangency to the $x$-axis.
- **C** and **E** each pick one sign. C needs $a>0$ and E needs $a<0$. Each is sufficient but not necessary, since the
  graph shows both cases: $a=2,\ b=4,\ c=4$ satisfies C but not E, and $a=-2,\ b=4,\ c=4$ satisfies E but not C.
- **D** and **F** square to $a^{2}=4c$ again, so they describe the $x$-axis. They are not even sufficient:
  $a=4,\ b=2,\ c=4$ satisfies D, and the circle has centre $(-2,-1)$ and radius $1$, which misses the $y$-axis.
:::

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
Which one of the following is a **necessary and sufficient** condition for

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin\left(\frac{k\pi}{3}\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$$

to be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $n=1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $n$ is a multiple of $3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $n$ is a multiple of $6$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $6$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $6$ or $n$ is $2$ more than a multiple of $6$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.** Work out the sum for small $n$ and look for the cycle.

**Step 1: the terms repeat every $6$**, because $\sin$ has period $2\pi$ and $\tfrac{6\pi}{3}=2\pi$.

| $k$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin\tfrac{k\pi}{3}$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $0$ | $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $0$ |
| running sum | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $\sqrt3$ | $\sqrt3$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ | $0$ | $0$ |

**Step 2: the cycle.** After six terms the running sum is back at $0$, so the running sums repeat every $6$ as well.

**Step 3: read off the exact condition.** The sum equals $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ at $n=1$ and $n=4$ in each cycle, that is, at
$n=1,4,7,10,13,\dots$ These are exactly the numbers that are $1$ more than a multiple of $3$.

**The other options.**

- **A** and **E** are sufficient but not necessary: each misses $n=4$.
- **B** fails at $n=3$, where the sum is $\sqrt3$.
- **C** fails at $n=6$, where the sum is $0$.
- **F** fails at $n=2$, where the sum is $\sqrt3$.

*E is the tempting answer if you stop checking after the first cycle and do not spot the second value at $n=4$.*
:::

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q14</span>

::: {.question}
An arithmetic sequence $T$ has first term $a$ and common difference $d$, where $a$ and $d$ are non-zero integers.

Property $P$ is:

> For some positive integer $m$, the sum of the first $m$ terms of the sequence is equal to the sum of the first $2m$ terms
> of the sequence.

For example, when $a=11$ and $d=-2$, the sequence $T$ has property $P$, because

$$11+9+7+5=11+9+7+5+3+1+(-1)+(-3)$$

i.e. the sum of the first $4$ terms equals the sum of the first $8$ terms.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; For $T$ to have property $P$, it is sufficient that $ad<0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; For $T$ to have property $P$, it is necessary that $d$ is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** neither of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** I and II
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** First turn property $P$ into an equation.

**Step 1: the exact condition.** Using $S_m=\tfrac12m\bigl(2a+(m-1)d\bigr)$, the equation $S_m=S_{2m}$ is

$$\tfrac12m\bigl(2a+(m-1)d\bigr)=\tfrac12(2m)\bigl(2a+(2m-1)d\bigr).$$

Divide both sides by $\tfrac12m$, which is allowed because $m>0$:

$$2a+(m-1)d=4a+(4m-2)d .$$

Collect terms:

$$2a+(3m-1)d=0 .$$

So $T$ has property $P$ exactly when this equation has a **positive integer** solution $m$.

*Check with the example:* $a=11$, $d=-2$ gives $22-2(3m-1)=0$, so $m=4$. ✓

**Step 2: test I.** I says $ad<0\Rightarrow P$. To break it, look for $ad<0$ where $m$ is not a positive integer. Take
$a=1$, $d=-2$. Then

$$2-2(3m-1)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ 3m-1=1\ \Longrightarrow\ m=\tfrac23,$$

which is not an integer. So $ad=-2<0$ but $T$ has no property $P$: the sequence $1,-1,-3,\dots$ falls too quickly. I is
false.

**Step 3: test II.** II says $P\Rightarrow d$ even. To break it, find a sequence with property $P$ and $d$ odd. Take $a=1$,
$d=-1$, so $T$ is $1,0,-1,\dots$ With $m=1$ the sum of the first term is $1$, and the sum of the first two terms is
$1+0=1$. So $T$ has property $P$, yet $d=-1$ is odd. II is false.

Neither holds, so **A**.

*The example in the stem has $ad<0$ and an even $d$, and both statements generalise from it. One worked example is
not evidence for either.*
:::

---

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following is a **sufficient** condition on the real constant $k$ for the equation

$$(x+k)^{1/2}+(x-k)^{1/4}=k$$

to have at least one real solution for $x$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $k=0$ or $k>3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $k=1$ or $k>3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $k=0$ or $1<k<3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $k\ge1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $0\le k\le3$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** Find the exact set of $k$, then look for the option inside it.

**Step 1: $k<0$ is impossible.** Both roots are non-negative, so the left side is at least $0$. It cannot equal a negative
number.

**Step 2: $k=0$ works.** The equation is $x^{1/2}+x^{1/4}=0$, and $x=0$ solves it.

**Step 3: $k>0$.** Both roots must be defined, so $x\ge k$. On that domain each root increases with $x$, so the left side
is **increasing**, and it grows without limit. Its smallest value is at $x=k$:

$$(2k)^{1/2}+0^{1/4}=\sqrt{2k}.$$

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.8,5.6))
for ax,k,title in [(axes[0],1,'$k=1$: the curve starts above $y=k$, so no solution'),(axes[1],3,'$k=3$: the curve starts below $y=k$, so it crosses')]:
    x=np.linspace(k,k+6,500)
    ax.plot(x,np.sqrt(x+k)+(x-k)**0.25,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='left side')
    ax.axhline(k,color='#d62728',lw=1.6,ls='--',label='$y=k$')
    ax.plot([k],[np.sqrt(2*k)],'o',color='#1f77b4',ms=5)
    ax.annotate(r'$\sqrt{2k}$',(k,np.sqrt(2*k)),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-26,6),fontsize=10)
    ax.set_title(title,fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=9,loc='lower right')
    ax.set_ylim(0,6); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.5); plt.show()
```

So a solution exists exactly when the smallest value is not above $k$:

$$\sqrt{2k}\le k\iff2k\le k^{2}\iff k\ge2\quad(\text{dividing by }k>0).$$

**Step 4: the exact set is** $k=0$ or $k\ge2$.

**Step 5: compare.** A sufficient condition must lie **inside** that set.

- **A** does: $k=0$ is in it, and every $k>3$ is in it.
- **B** contains $k=1$, which is outside.
- **C** contains $k=1.5$, which is outside.
- **D** and **E** both contain $k=1$, which is outside.

A is not necessary, since $k=2$ also works, but the question asks only for sufficient.
:::

---

# Section C — Polynomials, derivatives and integrals

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statements for real values of $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A:** $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin kx\,dx=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B:** $k$ is an even integer

Which one of the following is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** A is necessary but not sufficient for B

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** A is sufficient but not necessary for B

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** A is necessary and sufficient for B

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** A is not necessary and not sufficient for B
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** Both statements are really about $k$, although the stem says "real values of $x$". Do not confuse the statements
A and B with the option letters.

**Is A necessary for B?** That asks whether B $\Rightarrow$ A. If $k$ is an even integer (or any non-zero integer), then
$\sin kx$ completes $k$ whole cycles on $[0,2\pi]$, and over each cycle the area above and below the axis cancel. So the
integral is $0$. **Yes.**

**Is A sufficient for B?** That asks whether A $\Rightarrow$ B. An odd $k$ cancels as well. For $k=1$, the integral of
$\sin x$ over $[0,2\pi]$ is $0$, yet $k$ is not even. **No.**

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.8,4.8))
x=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,800)
for ax,k in [(axes[0],1),(axes[1],2)]:
    y=np.sin(k*x)
    ax.plot(x,y,color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
    ax.fill_between(x,y,0,where=y>=0,color='#2ca02c',alpha=.25,interpolate=True)
    ax.fill_between(x,y,0,where=y<=0,color='#d62728',alpha=.25,interpolate=True)
    ax.axhline(0,color='0.4',lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f'$k={k}$: the two colours cancel, so the integral is $0$',fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([0,np.pi,2*np.pi]); ax.set_xticklabels(['$0$',r'$\pi$',r'$2\pi$'])
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.5); plt.show()
```

**Algebra check.** For $k\ne0$,

$$\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin kx\,dx=\left[-\frac{\cos kx}{k}\right]_{0}^{2\pi}=\frac{1-\cos2\pi k}{k},$$

which is $0$ exactly when $k$ is an integer. So A is the larger set, the even integers sit inside it, and the
weaker statement is the necessary one.
:::

---

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement about the polynomial $\mathrm p(x)$, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers with $a<b$:

> $(*)$ There exists a number $c$ with $a<c<b$ such that $\mathrm p'(c)=0$.

Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The condition $\mathrm p(a)=\mathrm p(b)$ is necessary and sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The condition $\mathrm p(a)=\mathrm p(b)$ is necessary but not sufficient for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The condition $\mathrm p(a)=\mathrm p(b)$ is sufficient but not necessary for $(*)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The condition $\mathrm p(a)=\mathrm p(b)$ is not necessary and not sufficient for $(*)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

**Is the condition sufficient?** Suppose $\mathrm p(a)=\mathrm p(b)$. There are three cases for how the graph leaves
$x=a$.

- If it goes up, it must come back down to reach the same height at $x=b$, so it turns somewhere in between.
- If it goes down, it must come back up, so again it turns.
- If it does neither, the polynomial is constant, and then $\mathrm p'=0$ everywhere.

In every case a $c$ exists, so **yes**.

**Is the condition necessary?** We need a polynomial with a stationary point strictly between $a$ and $b$, but with
different heights at the ends. Take $\mathrm p(x)=x^{2}$, $a=-1$, $b=2$:

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.4))
x=np.linspace(-1.5,2.4,300)
ax.plot(x,x**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
ax.plot([-1,2],[1,4],'o',color='#d62728',ms=6); ax.plot([0],[0],'o',color='#2ca02c',ms=6)
ax.annotate('$p(-1)=1$',(-1,1),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-26,-18),fontsize=9)
ax.annotate('$p(2)=4$',(2,4),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(-52,0),fontsize=9)
ax.annotate("$p'(0)=0$",(0,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(8,8),fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=1); ax.axvline(0,color='0.5',lw=1)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Here $\mathrm p'(0)=0$ with $-1<0<2$, so $(*)$ holds, yet $\mathrm p(-1)=1\neq4=\mathrm p(2)$. So **no**.

Sufficient but not necessary is **C**.
:::

---

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statements about a polynomial $\mathrm f(x)$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $\mathrm f(x)=px^{3}+qx^{2}+rx+s$, where $p\neq0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; There is a real number $t$ for which $\mathrm f'(t)=0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; There are real numbers $u$ and $v$ for which $\mathrm f(u)\,\mathrm f(v)<0$.

Which of these statements is/are **sufficient** for the equation $\mathrm f(x)=0$ to have a real solution?

| | Statement I is sufficient | Statement II is sufficient | Statement III is sufficient |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **B** | Yes | Yes | No |
| **C** | Yes | No | Yes |
| **D** | Yes | No | No |
| **E** | No | Yes | Yes |
| **F** | No | Yes | No |
| **G** | No | No | Yes |
| **H** | No | No | No |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** Test each statement alone: does it **guarantee** a real root?

**I: yes.** A cubic with $p\ne0$ runs off to $+\infty$ at one end and $-\infty$ at the other. A polynomial's graph has no
breaks, so it must cross the $x$-axis.

**II: no.** Take $\mathrm f(x)=x^{2}+1$. Then $\mathrm f'(0)=0$, so II holds, but $x^{2}+1=0$ has no real solution.

**III: yes.** $\mathrm f(u)\,\mathrm f(v)<0$ means one value is positive and the other negative. So the graph has points on
both sides of the axis, and because a polynomial's graph is unbroken, it crosses between $u$ and $v$.

So the row is Yes, No, Yes, which is **C**.

*III needs "polynomial". The function $\tfrac1x$ has $\mathrm f(-1)\,\mathrm f(1)<0$ and no root at all, because its graph
is broken at $0$.*
:::

---

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following two statements about the polynomial $\mathrm f(x)$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**P:** $\mathrm f(x)=0$ for exactly three real values of $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Q:** $\mathrm f'(x)=0$ for exactly two real values of $x$

Which one of the following is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** P is necessary but not sufficient for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** P is sufficient but not necessary for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** P is necessary and sufficient for Q.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** P is not necessary and not sufficient for Q.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.** You need **two** counterexamples, one for each arrow.

**P is not necessary (Q does not give P).** A cubic with a repeated root has two stationary points but only two roots.
Take

$$\mathrm f(x)=x^{2}(x-3)=x^{3}-3x^{2},\qquad\mathrm f'(x)=3x^{2}-6x=3x(x-2).$$

The derivative is zero exactly at $x=0$ and $x=2$, so Q holds. The roots are $x=0$ and $x=3$ only, so P fails.

**P is not sufficient (P does not give Q).** Between consecutive roots there must be a stationary point, but nothing
stops there being **more** elsewhere. A degree-$5$ curve can wiggle above the axis without crossing it. For example,

$$\mathrm f(x)=3x^{5}-25x^{3}+60x+36,\qquad\mathrm f'(x)=15(x-2)(x-1)(x+1)(x+2).$$

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,axes=plt.subplots(2,1,figsize=(5.8,6.4))
x=np.linspace(-1,3.4,400)
ax=axes[0]; ax.plot(x,x**3-3*x**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
ax.plot([0,2],[0,-4],'o',color='#d62728',ms=5,label='stationary points (two)')
ax.plot([3],[0],'o',color='#2ca02c',ms=5,label='other root')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=1); ax.set_ylim(-6,4)
ax.set_title('$y=x^3-3x^2$: Q true, P false (only two roots)',fontsize=10); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=8.5,loc='upper left')
x=np.linspace(-2.6,2.7,600); f=lambda t:3*t**5-25*t**3+60*t+36
ax=axes[1]; ax.plot(x,f(x),color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
ax.plot([-2,-1,1,2],[f(-2),f(-1),f(1),f(2)],'o',color='#d62728',ms=5,label='stationary points (four)')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=1); ax.set_ylim(-25,110)
ax.set_title('$y=3x^5-25x^3+60x+36$: P true, Q false (three roots)',fontsize=10); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=8.5,loc='upper left')
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False); ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.45); plt.show()
```

The stationary values are $\mathrm f(-2)=20$, $\mathrm f(-1)=-2$, $\mathrm f(1)=74$, $\mathrm f(2)=52$. Only the dip at
$x=-1$ goes below the axis, so the curve crosses exactly three times, near $x\approx-2.39,\,-1.22,\,-0.79$. P holds and
Q fails, since there are four stationary points.

You are not expected to build this exact quintic. The idea is enough: a higher-degree curve can have extra wiggles that do
not reach the axis.

Neither arrow holds, so **D**.

*The tempting wrong answer is C, from picturing only the usual cubic with three roots and two turning points.*
:::

---

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q14</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statements about the polynomial $\mathrm p(x)$, where $a<b$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $\mathrm p(a)\le\mathrm p(b)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $\mathrm p'(a)\le\mathrm p'(b)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $\mathrm p''(a)\le\mathrm p''(b)$

Which of these statements is a **necessary** condition for $\mathrm p(x)$ to be increasing for $a\le x\le b$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** Necessary means: whenever $\mathrm p$ is increasing on $[a,b]$, the statement must hold. So to reject a statement,
find an increasing polynomial where it fails.

**I is necessary.** If $\mathrm p$ is increasing from $a$ to $b$, then its value at $b$ cannot be below its value at $a$.

**II is not necessary.** A curve can be increasing while its gradient **falls**. Take $\mathrm p(x)=9-x^{2}$ on
$[-3,0]$. Here $\mathrm p'(x)=-2x\ge0$ on this interval, so $\mathrm p$ is increasing. But

$$\mathrm p'(-3)=6,\qquad\mathrm p'(0)=0,$$

so $\mathrm p'(a)>\mathrm p'(b)$ and II fails.

**III is not necessary.** A quadratic cannot break III, because its $\mathrm p''$ is constant. So use a cubic. Take
$\mathrm p(x)=x-\tfrac16x^{3}$ on $[0,1]$. Then

$$\mathrm p'(x)=1-\tfrac12x^{2}>0\quad\text{on }[0,1],$$

so $\mathrm p$ is increasing, while $\mathrm p''(x)=-x$ gives $\mathrm p''(0)=0$ and $\mathrm p''(1)=-1$. So
$\mathrm p''(a)>\mathrm p''(b)$ and III fails.

Only I, so **B**.

*"Increasing" is about the values of $\mathrm p$. It says nothing about whether the gradient is itself rising, which is the
same mix-up as reading $f''>0$ as "the function is going up".*
:::

---

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statements about the polynomial $f(x)$, where $a<b$:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $f(a)>f(b)$;

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** $f'(x)\le0$ for all $x\in[a,b]$;

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx\le0$;

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** $f(a)+f(b)\le2f\left(\dfrac{a+b}{2}\right)$.

Which of these statements is a **necessary** condition for $f(x)$ to be decreasing for $a\le x\le b$? Here, decreasing means
that $x_1\le x_2$ implies $f(x_1)\ge f(x_2)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Only 1.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Only 2.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Only 3.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Only 4.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** Only 1 and 2.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** Only 1 and 3.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** Only 1 and 4.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** Only 2 and 3.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** Only 2 and 4.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** Take a decreasing polynomial and ask which statements it is forced to satisfy.

**(1) is not necessary.** Under the given definition a constant counts as decreasing. For $f(x)=1$ we have
$f(a)=f(b)$, so the strict inequality fails.

**(2) is necessary.** The gradient at $x$ is the limit of $\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ as $h\to0$. If $f$ is decreasing,
every such fraction with $h>0$ inside the interval is $\le0$, because the top is $\le0$. A limit of numbers $\le0$ is $\le0$, so
$f'(x)\le0$.

**(3) is not necessary.** Decreasing says nothing about the height of the curve. For $f(x)=1-x$ on $[0,1]$,

$$\int_{0}^{1}(1-x)\,dx=\frac12>0.$$

**(4) is not necessary.** This statement is about curvature, not direction. For $f(x)=x^{2}$ on $[-1,0]$, which is decreasing,

$$f(-1)+f(0)=1,\qquad2f\left(-\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac12,$$

and $1\le\tfrac12$ is false.

Only (2), so **C**.
:::

---

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
The function $\mathrm f(x)$ is defined for all real values of $x$.

Which of the following conditions on $\mathrm f(x)$ is/are **necessary** to ensure that

$$\int_{-5}^{0}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{5}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx\ ?$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Condition I:** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(-x)$ for $-5\le x\le5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Condition II:** $\mathrm f(x)=c$ for $-5\le x\le5$, where $c$ is a constant

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Condition III:** $\mathrm f(x)=-\mathrm f(-x)$ for $-5\le x\le5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** Necessary means: every function satisfying the integral equation must satisfy the condition. So for each condition,
find a function that satisfies the integral equation but breaks that condition.

**$\mathrm f(x)=x^{2}$ breaks II and III.** Both integrals equal $\tfrac{125}{3}$, so the equation holds. But $x^{2}$ is not
constant, and $x^{2}\ne-(-x)^{2}$ in general.

**$\mathrm f(x)=\sin2\pi x$ breaks I.** It has five full periods on each of $[-5,0]$ and $[0,5]$, so both integrals are $0$
and the equation holds. But it is odd, not even, so $\mathrm f(x)\ne\mathrm f(-x)$ in general.

So none of the three is necessary.

**The trap.** I and II are **sufficient**: an even function and a constant both force the two areas to be equal. Answering
E treats sufficient as if it were necessary, which is exactly what the wording is testing.
:::

---

## Question 20 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
$f(x)$ is a function defined for all real values of $x$.

Which one of the following is a **sufficient** condition for $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}f(x)\,dx=0$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(2)=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(1)=f(3)=0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x+2)=-f(2-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x-2)=-f(2-x)$ for all $x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.** Sufficient means the condition must **force** the integral to be $0$. So a single function that satisfies the
condition with a non-zero integral rules it out.

**A fails.** $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}$ has $f(2)=0$, but $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}(x-2)^{2}\,dx=\tfrac23$.

**B fails.** $f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$ has $f(1)=f(3)=0$, but $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}(x-1)(x-3)\,dx=-\tfrac43$.

**C fails.** $f(x)=x$ satisfies $f(-x)=-f(x)$, but $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3}x\,dx=4$. The condition controls $f$ about $x=0$,
which is not the middle of $[1,3]$.

**E fails.** Write $y=x-2$. Then $2-x=-y$, and E becomes $f(y)=-f(-y)$, which is condition C again in disguise. So $f(x)=x$
breaks it too.

**D works.** Read $f(2+x)=-f(2-x)$ as: the height at distance $x$ to the right of $2$ is minus the height at distance $x$ to
the left. That is rotational symmetry about the point $(2,0)$, the middle of $[1,3]$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.4))
x=np.linspace(0.7,3.3,400); g=lambda t:(t-2)**3-(t-2)+0.6*np.sin(np.pi*(t-2))
y=g(x); ax.plot(x,y,color='#1f77b4',lw=2)
xs=np.linspace(1,3,300); ys=g(xs)
ax.fill_between(xs,ys,0,where=ys>=0,color='#2ca02c',alpha=.25,interpolate=True)
ax.fill_between(xs,ys,0,where=ys<=0,color='#d62728',alpha=.25,interpolate=True)
ax.plot([2],[0],'o',color='k',ms=5); ax.annotate('$(2,0)$',(2,0),textcoords='offset points',xytext=(6,8),fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.5',lw=1); ax.axvline(1,color='0.7',lw=1,ls=':'); ax.axvline(3,color='0.7',lw=1,ls=':')
ax.set_xticks([1,2,3]); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title('Rotational symmetry about $(2,0)$: the two areas cancel',fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

So the area on $[2,3]$ exactly cancels the area on $[1,2]$:

$$\int_{1}^{3}f(x)\,dx=\int_{-1}^{1}f(2+t)\,dt=0,$$

because $f(2+t)$ is an odd function of $t$.

*Note that the official answer comes by elimination too. To show a condition is sufficient, checking one function that
satisfies the integral is not enough; that tests necessity instead.*
:::

---

# Section D — Symmetry and transformations

## Question 21 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The function $\mathrm f(x)$ is defined for all real numbers.

Consider the following three conditions, where $a$ is a real constant:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $\mathrm f(a-x)=\mathrm f(a+x)$ for all real $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $\mathrm f(2a-x)=\mathrm f(x)$ for all real $x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $\mathrm f(a-x)=\mathrm f(x)$ for all real $x$.

Which of these conditions is/are **necessary and sufficient** for the graph of $y=\mathrm f(x)$ to have reflection symmetry
in the line $x=a$?

| | Condition I is | Condition II is | Condition III is |
|---|---|---|---|
| | necessary and sufficient | necessary and sufficient | necessary and sufficient |
| **A** | yes | yes | yes |
| **B** | yes | yes | no |
| **C** | yes | no | yes |
| **D** | yes | no | no |
| **E** | no | yes | yes |
| **F** | no | yes | no |
| **G** | no | no | yes |
| **H** | no | no | no |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** Reflection in $x=a$ means: two points the **same distance** from $a$, on opposite sides, have the same height.

**I: yes.** The inputs $a-x$ and $a+x$ are at distance $|x|$ on either side of $a$. Letting $x$ run over all reals covers every
such pair, so I says precisely that the graph is symmetric.

**II: yes.** The inputs $2a-x$ and $x$ have midpoint $\dfrac{(2a-x)+x}{2}=a$, so they are also mirror images in $x=a$. In fact,
replacing $x$ with $a+x$ turns II into

$$\mathrm f(a-x)=\mathrm f(a+x),$$

which is I.

**III: no.** The inputs $a-x$ and $x$ have midpoint $\tfrac a2$, so III describes symmetry in the line $x=\tfrac a2$, a
different line unless $a=0$.

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.4))
a=2; x=np.linspace(-1.2,5.2,400)
ax.plot(x,(x-a)**2,color='#1f77b4',lw=2,label='$y=(x-2)^2$')
ax.axvline(a,color='#2ca02c',ls='--',lw=1.4,label='mirror line $x=a=2$')
ax.axvline(a/2,color='#d62728',ls=':',lw=1.4,label='the line III describes, $x=a/2=1$')
ax.plot([0,4],[4,4],'o',color='#2ca02c',ms=5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.5,9); ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.legend(frameon=False,fontsize=8.5,loc='upper center',bbox_to_anchor=(0.5,-0.18),ncol=1)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*A counterexample for III:* with $a=2$, the graph $\mathrm f(x)=(x-2)^{2}$ is symmetric in $x=2$, but $\mathrm f(2-x)=x^{2}$, which is not
$\mathrm f(x)$. So III is not necessary.

The row is yes, yes, no, which is **B**.
:::

## Question 22 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
When the graph of the function $y=\mathrm f(x)$, defined on the real numbers, is reflected in the $y$-axis and then translated by
$2$ units in the negative $x$-direction, the result is the graph of the function $y=\mathrm g(x)$.

When the graph of the same function $y=\mathrm f(x)$ is translated by $2$ units in the negative $x$-direction and then reflected in
the $y$-axis, the result is the graph of the function $y=\mathrm h(x)$.

Which one of the following conditions on $y=\mathrm f(x)$ is **necessary and sufficient** for the functions $\mathrm g(x)$ and
$\mathrm h(x)$ to be identical?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(x+2)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(x+4)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(x+8)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(2-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(4-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $\mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(8-x)$ for all $x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** Write down $\mathrm g$ and $\mathrm h$ exactly. Each transformation replaces $x$ in the current formula.

**Step 1: find $\mathrm g$.** Reflecting in the $y$-axis replaces $x$ by $-x$, giving $\mathrm f(-x)$. Translating $2$ units in the
negative $x$-direction replaces $x$ by $x+2$:

$$\mathrm g(x)=\mathrm f(-(x+2))=\mathrm f(-x-2).$$

**Step 2: find $\mathrm h$.** Translating first gives $\mathrm f(x+2)$. Reflecting replaces $x$ by $-x$:

$$\mathrm h(x)=\mathrm f(-x+2).$$

**Step 3: set them equal for all $x$.**

$$\mathrm f(-x-2)=\mathrm f(-x+2)\quad\text{for all }x.$$

Let $u=-x-2$. As $x$ runs over all reals, so does $u$, and $-x+2=u+4$. So the condition is exactly

$$\mathrm f(u)=\mathrm f(u+4)\quad\text{for all }u.$$

Every step reverses, so this is necessary **and** sufficient.

**The other options.**

- **A** (period $2$) is sufficient but not necessary: $\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{2}$ has period $4$ but not period $2$.
- **C** (period $8$) is necessary but not sufficient: $\sin\tfrac{\pi x}{4}$ has period $8$ but not period $4$.
- **D**, **E**, **F**, **G** are mirror symmetries, not periods. A parabola with the matching axis satisfies each of them, and
  a parabola is not periodic, so $\mathrm g\ne\mathrm h$.
:::

---

## Question 23 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
Three transformations of the plane are defined as follows. $R$ is the reflection in the $y$-axis. $T$ is the translation by $4$
units in the positive $x$-direction. $S$ is the horizontal stretch with scale factor $2$ parallel to the $x$-axis, fixing the
$y$-axis.

Let $y=f(x)$ be a function defined on the real numbers.

When the graph of $y=f(x)$ is transformed by applying $R$, then $T$, then $S$ in that order, the result is the graph of
$y=g(x)$.

When the graph of the same function $y=f(x)$ is transformed by applying $S$, then $T$, then $R$ in that order, the result is
the graph of $y=h(x)$.

Which one of the following conditions on $y=f(x)$ is **necessary and sufficient** for the functions $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ to be
identical?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(x)=f(x+3)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(x)=f(x+4)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x)=f(x+6)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x)=f(x+12)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)=f(-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(x)=f(6-x)$ for all $x$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** Apply each transformation to the formula in turn. Each one replaces $x$ in the **current** formula.

| Step | Rule | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| $R$ | $x\to-x$ | $f(-x)$ |
| $T$ | $x\to x-4$ | $f(-(x-4))=f(4-x)$ |
| $S$ | $x\to\tfrac x2$ | $g(x)=f\left(4-\tfrac x2\right)$ |

| Step | Rule | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| $S$ | $x\to\tfrac x2$ | $f\left(\tfrac x2\right)$ |
| $T$ | $x\to x-4$ | $f\left(\tfrac{x-4}{2}\right)=f\left(\tfrac x2-2\right)$ |
| $R$ | $x\to-x$ | $h(x)=f\left(-\tfrac x2-2\right)$ |

**Set them equal.** We need $f\left(4-\tfrac x2\right)=f\left(-\tfrac x2-2\right)$ for all $x$.

Let $u=-\tfrac x2-2$. As $x$ runs over all reals, so does $u$, and $4-\tfrac x2=u+6$. So the condition is exactly

$$f(u+6)=f(u)\quad\text{for all }u.$$

**The other options.**

- **A** (period $3$) is sufficient but not necessary, since period $3$ gives period $6$, but period $6$ does not give period $3$.
- **D** (period $12$) is necessary but not sufficient.
- **B** (period $4$) neither gives nor follows from period $6$.
- **E** and **F** are mirror symmetries. A parabola satisfies them without being periodic.
:::

---

## Question 24 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a function defined on the real numbers.

When the graph of $y=f(x)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis and then stretched in the $x$-direction by a factor of $\tfrac12$, the
result is the graph of $y=g(x)$.

When the graph of $y=f(x)$ is stretched in the $x$-direction by a factor of $\tfrac12$ and then translated by $1$ unit in the
negative $x$-direction, the result is the graph of $y=h(x)$.

Which of the following is a **sufficient but not necessary condition** for $g(x)$ and $h(x)$ to be identical, that is
$g(x)=h(x)$ for all real values of $x$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(0)=f(2)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(x)=f(2-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x+1)=f(1-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x)=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}\cos(\pi kx)$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)=f(1-x)$ for all $x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(x)=\cos(\pi x)+\sin(\pi x)$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.** Find the exact condition, then look for an option strictly inside it.

**Step 1: find $g$ and $h$.** Stretching in the $x$-direction by a factor of $\tfrac12$ replaces $x$ by $2x$.

- $g$: reflect to get $f(-x)$, then stretch: $g(x)=f(-2x)$.
- $h$: stretch to get $f(2x)$, then translate by replacing $x$ with $x+1$: $h(x)=f(2(x+1))=f(2x+2)$.

**Step 2: the exact condition.** We need $f(-2x)=f(2x+2)$ for all $x$. Let $u=-2x$, which runs over all reals. Then $2x+2=2-u$, so

$$g=h\iff f(u)=f(2-u)\quad\text{for all }u.$$

The graph must be symmetric in the line $x=1$.

**Step 3: the options.**

- **B** is exactly this condition. It is necessary **and** sufficient, so it is not "not necessary".
- **C** is the same condition: put $u=x+1$, and $1-x$ becomes $2-u$.
- **A** checks a single pair of points, so it is not sufficient. For $f(x)=x(x-1)(x-2)$, we have $f(0)=f(2)$, but
  $f(2-x)=-f(x)$, which is not $f(x)$.
- **E** is symmetry in $x=\tfrac12$, the wrong line. $f(x)=\left(x-\tfrac12\right)^{2}$ satisfies E but not the exact condition.
- **F** is not sufficient. Since $\sin(\pi(2-x))=-\sin(\pi x)$, we get $f(2-x)=\cos\pi x-\sin\pi x\neq f(x)$.
- **D** works. For each $k$,

$$\cos(\pi k(2-x))=\cos(2\pi k-\pi kx)=\cos(\pi kx),$$

so every term, and therefore the sum, is symmetric in $x=1$. So D is **sufficient**. It is one specific function, while
$f(x)=(x-1)^{2}$ also satisfies the exact condition and is not this sum, so D is **not necessary**.

*The unusual feature here is that a sufficient condition can be a single function. Any function with the symmetry is
strictly inside the exact set.*
:::
